title: The Pratfall Effect
description: A competent person becomes more likeable after making a small blunder, because it humanizes them and reduces perceived threat.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: A competent person becomes more likeable after making a small blunder, because it humanizes them and reduces perceived threat.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: The polished CEO who spills coffee on himself just before speaking suddenly seems more relatable.
A brilliant colleague admits a silly mistake and the team warms to her more than before.
An interviewer trips over a chair; the candidate becomes less nervous because the authority figure now seems fallible.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: A visible imperfection after a string of flawless performances.
Audiences relaxing after a speaker makes a minor error.

sections.title: Warning Signs (of strategic use)
content: The mistake conveniently arrives right when the person needs to be more relatable.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Competent people can intimidate. A pratfall signals safety and approachability, increasing likability without undermining the perception of competence. Aronson, Willerman, & Floyd (1966) found that a highly competent person who committed a blunder was rated as more attractive than one who was flawless.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Distinguish genuine human moments from calculated manipulation. If it feels too perfectly imperfect, it might be.
Don’t lower your evaluation of someone’s ability just because you like them more after a mistake.
Remember that competence and likeability are independent.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Using the effect as an excuse to be sloppy; it only works if you’re already perceived as highly competent.
Over-apologizing after a minor error, which turns a pratfall into a larger issue.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A new project leader delivers a flawless presentation. The team is impressed but distant. The next day, she accidentally sends an email to the wrong group and immediately sends a light-hearted apology. Suddenly, she seems approachable, and team members start confiding in her.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Perfection creates distance. A small crack can be the door that lets people in.
